title: Moafee
summary: Moafee is a low-volume espionage cluster that public reporting first described in 2014 after intrusions against defence contractors and their suppliers. The reporting described spear phishing messages carrying malicious documents, followed by remote access tools that gave operators interactive control of a workstation. The tradecraft looked less mature than that of the well-documented state espionage units of the same period: infrastructure was reused, tooling overlapped with other clusters, and individual campaigns were small. That overlap is the main analytic problem, because shared tools and shared hosting can make two unrelated groups look like one. Evidence in an environment is usually a phishing attachment that executed a script, a scheduled task or service created shortly afterwards, and periodic outbound connections to a small set of hosts. Public analysis of this cluster has always been limited, and vendors have disagreed about whether the activity is a distinct group, part of a larger cluster, or a set of unrelated intrusions.

beginner.definition: Moafee is the name given to a small group of attackers who targeted defence companies. Security researchers wrote about it in 2014. Very little public information exists about the group, so even experts are not sure who was behind it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Small groups still cause serious damage. They often use cheap, well-known tools, so they are hard to tell apart from other attackers. If your team only hunts for famous groups, this kind of quiet intrusion can stay on your network for a long time.
howItWorks: The attackers send email that looks like a normal business message to a small number of employees.
The message asks the reader to open an attached document or to click a link.
Opening the file starts a hidden script instead of showing ordinary document content.
The script downloads a remote control program and sets it to start again after each restart.
The operator then uses that program to look at files and at other computers on the network.
beginner.example: Imagine a small office where everyone knows the delivery driver. One day a stranger in the same uniform hands over a parcel, and the receptionist signs for it without a second look. Nobody checks the paperwork carefully, because parcels arrive every morning. The box sits in the storeroom for weeks, quietly copying whatever passes nearby. When files go missing months later, nobody connects the loss to that ordinary morning delivery.
takeaways: Unknown groups still matter, because they often reuse tools that are easy to detect.
An email attachment that asks you to enable content deserves a second look.
Limited public reporting means attribution claims should be treated with care.

objectives: Explain why a low-profile threat group is harder to attribute than a well-documented one.
Describe how a phishing document leads to a persistent remote access tool.
Identify the host artefacts that appear after a malicious office document runs.
Explain why shared tooling can cause analysts to merge two separate groups.
Describe how limited public reporting affects the confidence of an assessment.
